opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The Law required priests to work on the Sabbath. They offered sacrifices, changed the bread of the Presence, maintained the Temple, and carried out worship. Technically, they were doing labor on the very day labor was forbidden. Yet they were innocent because their work was in service of God. The Temple itself made that work holy.

Then Jesus says this:

“I say to you, something greater than the temple is here.”

He is speaking about Himself.  To the Jewish people, the Temple was the dwelling place of God’s presence. By saying He is greater than the Temple, Jesus is claiming that God’s presence is now found in Him. If the Temple gave priests authority to work on the Sabbath, then the Son of God has even greater authority over the Sabbath.
A few verses later:

“For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” (Matthew 12:8)

The deeper lesson is that the Pharisees had become so focused on rules that they missed the One to whom those rules pointed. The Sabbath was never intended to burden people but to draw them closer to God. Jesus fulfills the Law rather than abolishing it. Mercy, worship, and caring for others are not violations of God’s will—they are its fulfillment.

For us, this passage asks a challenging question:

* Do I cling to religious practices while missing Christ Himself?
* Do I use rules to judge others instead of showing mercy?
* Do I recognize that true rest is found in Jesus, not merely in observing regulations?

When Jesus says, “something greater than the temple is here,” He is inviting everyone to see that God’s presence is no longer centered in a building but in the person of Christ.
